newsitem.title: SYRIA: Assad says Syria committed to peace with Israel.
newsitem.headline: Assad says Syria committed to peace with Israel.

text.p: Syrian President Hafez al-Assad said after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Damascus on Saturday that Syria was still committed to make peace with Israel.

But the Syrian leader, addressing a joint news conference with Mubarak, accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of giving nothing to revive the Syrian-Israeli peace talks, suspended for about a year.

"He (Netanyahu) says he wants to resume the negotiations without pre-conditions. The word pre-conditions means that he is putting conditions...he speaks about restarting the talks from the zero point," Assad said.

He said the previous Labour-led Israeli government had agreed during sporadic talks with Syria to withdraw fully from the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in 1967, and that the talks should resume from this point.
Netanyahu, who defeated Labour, says he will not swap occupied Arab lands for peace, a formula on which the Arab-Israeli peace talks were based when they began in Madrid in 1991.
Assad said Arabs wanted peace with Israel and that talk about Arabs wanting to throw Jews in the sea was not made by any Arab official.

"We heard about throwing the Jews in the sea a long time ago, but I did not hear it from any Arab official. I personally tried to inquire about who said it in the past, but I did not find anybody...," Assad said.

"Even if we will fight each other. is throwing in the sea a solution? No, it is not the solution...anyway, we fought each other a lot but we did not throw each other in the sea," the Syrian leader said.
Assad and Mubarak said they did not receive any fresh peace ideas or proposals from Netanyahu following his visit to the United States and talks with President Bill Clinton earlier this month.
"We in Syria were not informed by anybody about anything. We heard statements," Assad said.
"I asked President Hafez al-Assad whether there was anything new and he said to me no, nothing yet," Mubarak said.

President Mubarak said he would discuss the peace process with Clinton during his forthcoming visit to Washington and to look at new ideas to push forward the peace talks on the Syrian and Lebanese tracks.
Both leaders criticised Israel's settlement policies and said it would complicate the peace process.
Mubarak, who was accompanied by a team including Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, returned home on Saturday after his short visit to Damascus.
